title: Propagation beyond the horizon
blurb: Explain how signals get past the horizon: refraction, the ionosphere, ducting, sporadic E, meteors and aurora.

T3C01.why: UHF is usually **not propagated by the ionosphere**, so with only line of sight it rarely goes beyond the radio horizon.
T3C01.trap: Nothing forbids range, and UHF isn't absorbed by the D region.

T3C02.why: The ionosphere reflects HF, so **long-distance ionospheric paths are far more common on HF**.
T3C02.trap: HF antennas are larger, not smaller.

T3C03.why: Aurora scatters and smears the signal, giving a **distorted, raspy** sound.

T3C04.why: Occasional strong 10, 6 and 2 m signals from beyond the horizon point to **sporadic E**.

T3C05.why: A sharp obstacle edge bends some signal around it: **knife-edge diffraction**.
T3C05.trap: Faraday rotation twists polarization; it doesn't get you past obstructions.

T3C06.why: Regular VHF/UHF contacts to about 300 miles come from **tropospheric ducting**.
T3C06.trap: D and F2 region refraction are ionospheric, and not what gives regular UHF range.

T3C07.why: Meteor scatter is best on **6 meters**.

T3C08.why: A layer of warm air over cool air, a **temperature inversion**, traps signals in a duct.
T3C08.trap: Storms and sunspots are not the cause.

T3C09.why: The F region is densest by day and near the sunspot peak: **dawn to shortly after sunset, high sunspot activity**.

T3C10.why: At the sunspot peak the F region bends **6 and 10 meters**. Higher VHF and UHF bands pass through.

T3C11.why: The atmosphere **refracts** radio waves slightly downward, so the radio horizon is beyond the visual one.
T3C11.trap: Radio waves never exceed the speed of light.
